*Application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of

and Arbour JJ.).

Human rights -- Discrimination -- Handicap -- Collective agreement providing that employees on unpaid leave of absence due to disability not accumulating seniority and service after periods set out in agreement and that employer not required to contribute premiums to employee benefit plans after employees had been receiving long-term disability benefits for specified periods of time -- Provisions of collective agreement with respect to service accrual and employer contributions not discriminating on basis of handicap contrary to
s. 5
of
Human Rights Code
-- Provisions with respect to seniority discriminating on basis of handicap -- Violation of s. 5 not excused under s. 17 of Code -- Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, ss. 5,
17
.
Under the central collective agreement between the parties, nurses on unpaid leave of absence due to disability did not accumulate seniority and service after the periods set out in the agreement and the employer was not required to contribute premiums to employee benefit plans after the employees had been receiving long-term disability payments for specified periods of time. An Arbitration Board held that the provisions respecting service accrual and subsidization of benefit plans did not discriminate on the basis of disability contrary to
s. 5
of the
Human Rights Code
, but that the provisions respecting seniority did contravene the Code. The union and the employers applied for judicial review of the award. The Divisional Court dismissed the application by the union and allowed the application of the employers, holding that none of the impugned provisions contravened the Code. The union appealed.
Held, the appeal should be allowed in part.
Employer contributions to benefit plans are a form of compensation. Providing different levels of compensation to different groups of employees is not itself discriminatory within the meaning of the Code. Prohibited discrimination only occurs when the distinction is based on a prohibited ground. The prohibited ground alleged in this case was handicap. Disabled nurses did not receive this compensation because they were not providing services to their employer. It is not prohibited discrimination to distinguish for purposes of compensation between employees who are providing services for the employer and those who are not. On its face, discrimination would exist if the employer provided different levels of compensation for work because of handicap or if the employer provided different levels of compensation for not working because of handicap. In this context, working employees could not be compared with those not working. The appropriate comparator group for handicapped employees who were not worki ng was employees who were not working for other reasons. The benefits provided to handicapped employees were more generous than those provided to other employees who were not providing work. Therefore, there was no discrimination on a prohibited basis within the meaning of s. 5(1) of the Code.
The union failed to demonstrate a contravention of s. 11 of the Code, which deals with constructive or adverse effect discrimination. Even if the rule respecting employer contributions to benefit plan premiums constituted constructive dismissal, the justification in s. 11(1)(b) of the Code for a bona fide occupational qualification applied. Requiring work in exchange for compensation is a reasonable and bona fide requirement.
The above analysis applied equally to service accrual. The purpose of service accrual is to fix the level of compensation on the salary grid and vacation pay. Accordingly, for the purposes of s. 5 of the Code, the appropriate comparator group was other employees on unpaid leave of absence. All employees within this group, handicapped and non-handicapped, were treated the same. Therefore, there was no s. 5 discrimination. For the reasons set out above, there was no constructive or adverse effect discrimination in respect of service accrual.
Under the collective agreement, accrual of seniority had a different purpose than service accrual or employer contributions to benefit premiums. Seniority was a consideration for the purpose of filling vacancies and determining the order in which employees were laid off and hired back, but it was not the only consideration. The principal considerations for filling vacancies were skill, experience and qualifications, and seniority was only the deciding factor where these other considerations were relatively equal among the competing employees. Similarly, for layoffs and recalls, seniority only governed if the most senior employees were qualified to perform the available work. Thus, in this collective agreement, seniority was not directly related to compensation. The purpose of seniority was not to provide an additional form of compensation in exchange for work. The seniority provisions were triggered simply by the status of being an employee, a status which long-term disabled employees retained. It followed that the relevant comparator group with respect to seniority was all other employees. In this agreement, seniority directly affected the ability of employees to access, remain in and thrive in the workplace. It was therefore a right that was at the core of human rights legislation as it affects the disabled. By depriving employees of seniority accrual over the periods when they were unable to work, the agreement put disabled employees at an unfair disadvantage by reason of their handicap. Disabled employees were denied rights which were given to other employees in a manner constituting discrimination within the meaning of s. 5 of the Code.
The violation of s. 5 was not excused under s. 17 of the Code. It was not shown that while on long-term disability, an employee was incapable of performing any essential duty or requirement relating to the accumulation of seniority. Seniority for full-time employees involved nothing more than the passage of time as an employee, a status that long-term disabled persons retained. The provisions denying handicapped workers the right to accumulate seniority while on long-term disability should be struck down.

The judgment of the court was delivered by

ROSENBERG J.A.: -- This appeal concerns the legality of
certain provisions of the central collective agreement produced
by collective bargaining between the Ontario Nurses'
Association and a number of hospitals in the province. The
respondent hospitals, Orillia Soldiers Memorial Hospital and
Sault Ste. Marie General Hospital, are parties to the
agreement. Each hospital employs one or more members of the ONA
who were on unpaid leave of absence due to disability. The ONA
argues that certain provisions in the collective agreement
discriminate on the basis of disability in contravention of the

Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19
.

The provisions at issue concern seniority, service accrual
and the employers' contribution to subsidized benefit plans. In
summary, while nurses on unpaid leave of absence remain
employees, they do not accumulate seniority and service after
the periods set out in the agreement. As well, the employer is
not required to contribute premiums to the benefit plans after
the employees have been receiving long-term disability payments
for specified periods of time. Three separate grievances were
filed when the hospitals acted in accordance with the
collective agreement. A majority of the Arbitration Board held
that the provisions respecting service accrual and
subsidization of benefit plans did not violate the
Human Rights
Code
. A different majority held that the provisions respecting
seniority did contravene the Code. The ONA and the hospitals
applied for judicial review of the award to the Divisional
Court. The Divisional Court dismissed the application by the
ONA and allowed the application o f the hospitals holding that
none of the impugned provisions contravened the Code.

I would allow the appeal in part and restore the award of the
Arbitration Board. I agree with the Board that only the
provisions respecting seniority contravene the
Human Rights
Code
.

THE FACTS

The arbitration proceeded on the basis of a very brief
statement of agreed facts and the collective agreement itself.
Although the parties must have known that the purpose of these
various impugned provisions was crucial to a determination of
this case, no evidence was led on these issues. In my view, a
more complete record would have been of considerable assistance
in resolving the issues on this appeal. I will return to my
concerns later in these reasons. The parties urged us to decide
this case on the basis of the record, such as it is, and I
have, with some reluctance, done so.

The Grievers

One griever is an employee of Orillia. Her last day of work
was in April 1990. After a period on short-term disability and
unemployment insurance benefits, she began receiving long-term
disability benefits. It was agreed that her disability falls
within the meaning of "handicap" in
s. 10(1)
(a) of the
Human
Rights Code
.

The other grievers are employees of Sault Ste. Marie. They
each suffered work-related injuries and were receiving
unemployment insurance, long-term disability payments or
workers' compensation benefits. Their disabilities also fall
within the term "handicap" as defined by the Code.

In the course of oral argument, we were informed that two of
the grievers have returned to work.

The Collective Agreement

This appeal principally concerns provisions in Articles 10
and 17 of the ONA Full-Time Collective Agreement in force
between 1991 and 1993. These provisions address four main
terms: employer contributions to benefits, service accrual,
seniority, and other employees on unpaid leave of absence. This
appeal deals mainly with the first three terms. The effects of
these provisions are set out in the chart below:
