Employer contributions to benefits

In accordance with art. 17.01, the employer is required to
make premium contributions to four health and welfare plans for
full-time employees. The percentage of the employer
contribution for active employees varies, depending on the
plan, from 100 per cent for semi-private hospital care, to 50
per cent of premiums for a dental plan. While a nurse is on
unpaid leave of absence, the employer continues to make premium
contributions for 30 days; thereafter the nurse pays 100 per
cent of the premiums. While a nurse is receiving workers'
compensation payments, the employer continues to make the same
contribution as if the nurse were an active employee (full
contributions). While a nurse is receiving long-term disability
payments, the hospital makes its contributions for the 30
months from the date absence commenced (art. 17.05);
thereafter, the nurse pays 100 per cent of the premiums.

The ONA argues that this difference in treatment between
nurses on unpaid leave of absence because of handicap and
active employees violates the Code. Before this court, counsel
for the ONA also argued that the difference in treatment
between employees on workers' compensation and employees in
receipt of long-term disability constituted a violation of the
Code. This issue was not raised before the Arbitration Board or
the Divisional Court. There is no evidentiary record on this
issue. On very short notice, counsel for the respondent, Mr.
Gray, in his helpful submissions, pointed out that this
distinction probably arises out of the special statutory regime
in force in Ontario that has removed workplace injuries from
the civil courts. In my view, the issue is not properly before
this court and I would not permit the ONA to raise it at this
stage.

Service accrual

The number of years of full-time continuous service is used
to calculate various forms of compensation such as paid
vacation (art. 16) and place on the wage grid (art. 19.01). A
nurse on unpaid leave of absence only accumulates service for
30 days (art. 10.04).

Seniority

Seniority is determined by a nurse's date of hire. Under the
agreement, nurses are laid off based on seniority, provided the
nurses who are entitled to remain (based on seniority) are
qualified to perform the available work. Nurses are also
recalled to work in the order of seniority. For nurses on
unpaid leave of absence and in receipt of workers' compensation
benefits or long-term disability benefits, seniority only
accrues for up to one year (art. 10.04).

Other employees on unpaid leave of absence

The benefits provided for disabled employees are the same as,
or exceed, benefits provided to most other employees on unpaid
leave of absence. For example, a nurse on unpaid leave of
absence by reason other than disability accumulates seniority
for 30 days, whereas disabled employees accumulate seniority
for a year. There are exceptions for nurses on pregnancy or
parental leave. For example, a nurse on pregnancy leave
accumulates service for 17 weeks rather than only 30 days. It
was not argued that this difference in treatment infringes the
Code. The collective agreement also includes special provisions
for paid leave of absence including short-term sick leave of up
to 15 weeks. Employees on short-term sick leave are treated as
active employees.

THE POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES

The position of the ONA is straightforward. Nurses on unpaid
leave of absence are treated differently from other employees
on active service. They are, however, all employees. Where the
reason for the absence is a handicap as defined in the
Human
Rights Code
, this group of employees is being discriminated
against on the basis of a ground prohibited by the Code. Having
established a prima facie violation of s. 11 of the Code, the
onus is on the employer to show that the needs of this group of
workers cannot be accommodated without undue hardship.

The position of the employers is similarly straightforward.
They argue that the Code right to equal treatment with respect
to employment without discrimination does not include the
provision of pay, benefits and other advantages when the
employee is not performing work. Where the employer does
provide pay, benefits or other advantages for employees who do
not perform work, the employer must do so in a manner that does
not discriminate on a prohibited ground, such as handicap. In
the cases before the court, the benefits and advantages
provided to disabled employees are the same as, or superior to,
the benefits and advantages provided to other employees who do
not perform work. Accordingly, there is no violation of the
Code.

In large part, this case is about determining the appropriate
group for comparison. The ONA argues that but for their
handicap these employees would be on active service and
therefore the appropriate comparator group is the group of
employees in the bargaining unit as a whole. The employers
argue that wages, benefits, and accumulation of service credits
and seniority do not flow simply from the employer/employee
relationship, but from the provision of work. Therefore, the
appropriate comparator group is all other employees not
providing work, not the bargaining unit as a whole, which
includes employees providing work.

THE QUESTIONS BEFORE THE BOARD

Before the Board, the parties agreed to frame the issues
arising out of the grievances in the form of the following
three questions:

A.  Are the collective agreement provisions relating to the
accrual of seniority and service for nurses absent
without pay from the hospital and in receipt of
benefits under the Workers' Compensation Act
discriminatory in contravention of the
Human Rights
Code
?

B.  Are the collective agreement provisions relating to the
accrual of seniority and service for nurses absent
without pay from the hospital and in receipt of
benefits under the disability income plan (HOODIP or an
equivalent plan) or in receipt of UI benefits
referenced in paragraph 7 [of the agreed facts],
discriminatory in contravention of the
Human Rights
Code
?

C.  Are the collective agreement provisions relating to the
hospital's continuing to pay its contributions to
benefit premiums for nurses absent and in receipt of
benefits under the disability income plan (HOODIP or an
equivalent plan) or in receipt of UI benefits
referenced in paragraph 7, discriminatory in
contravention of the
Human Rights Code
?

REASONS OF THE ARBITRATION BOARD

A majority of the Arbitration Board held that resolution of
these questions depended upon the application of the decision
of Arbitrator Brown in Versa Services Ltd. v. Milk & Bread
Drivers, Dairy Employees, Caterers & Allied Employees Union,
Local 647 (1994),
1994 CanLII 18586 (ON LA)
, 39 L.A.C. (4th) 196, affirmed by an
endorsement of the Divisional Court, delivered February 7,
1995. Versa Services concerned a collective agreement requiring
employees on long-term disability to pay the cost of benefits
if they wished to maintain coverage. The employer paid some or
all of the premiums for employees on active service. Arbitrator
Brown held that the right to employer benefit contributions was
in the nature of compensation and it was lawful for the
employer to treat employees differently for purposes of
compensation depending on whether or not they were working. I
will return to the Versa Services decision below.

The chair of the arbitration board in this case, Mr.
Mitchnik, and the employer nominee, Mr. Filion, held that the
reasoning in Versa Services applied not only to employer
benefit contributions but also to service accrual. Mr. Filion
would have held that the Versa Services reasoning also applied
to accumulation of seniority. Mr. Mitchnik held that seniority
accrual primarily concerned access to the workplace and was not
in the nature of compensation. Accordingly, he held that Versa
Services had no application and there was a violation of the
Code with respect to seniority accrual.

The union representative, Mr. Anand, held the Code was
violated in all three areas. He rejected the Versa Services
approach, believing the case was governed by another line of
cases dealing with deemed termination and represented by the
decision of the Divisional Court in Ontario Nurses' Assn. v.
Etobicoke General Hospital (1993),
1993 CanLII 8635 (ON CTGD)
, 14 O.R. (3d) 40, 104 D.L.R.
(4th) 379. That case concerned a clause in the collective
agreement that deemed all employees absent from work for more
than 24 months due to illness or disability to be automatically
terminated. The Divisional Court held that the automatic
termination clause violated the Code since it deprived handicap
employees of the right not to be discharged without a showing
of proper cause. Mr. Anand also found support for his position
in the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Ontario Human
Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536,
23 D.L.R. (4th) 321. In Simpsons-Sears, the court found a
violation of the Code when the employer discharged an employee
from full-time employment because she was unwilling to work on
Saturday because of her religious beliefs.

In sum, Mr. Mitchnik and Mr. Filion held that there was no
violation with respect to employer benefit contributions and
service accrual. Mr. Mitchnik and Mr. Anand found that the
provisions in the agreement respecting accrual of seniority
contravened the Code.

THE REASONS OF THE DIVISIONAL COURT

The Divisional Court (Hartt, Campbell and Caswell JJ.) held
that this case was determined by the decision in Versa
Services. The court considered that it should follow Versa
Services unless there was some strong reason to the contrary,
such as an indication that the panel failed to consider some
statutory provision or binding authority. The court found no
such reason. Thus the court held that Mr. Mitchnik was correct
in applying Versa Services to employer benefit contributions
and service accrual. However, the court agreed with Mr. Filion
that Versa Services also applied to accumulation of seniority
and adopted the following part of Mr. Filion's reasons:

Given that it is not discriminatory for the Collective
Agreement to limit an employee's entitlement to service
credits and benefit coverage when absent due to "handicap" it
follows, a fortiori, that it is not discriminatory for the
Agreement to limit an employee's accumulation of seniority
rights when absent for similar reasons. The fact that the
employer's interest in seniority accumulation may not be as
great as it is in relation to compensation issues is no basis
for the quantum leap which distinguishes the two concepts
from a human rights viewpoint. It is not logical to infer
that the drafters of the Code intended to create seniority
protection for employees off work due to illness or injury
where it clearly did not provide any similar protection for
the accumulation of service credits or benefit coverage.

THE ONTARIO HUMAN RIGHTS CODE PROVISIONS

Following are the relevant provisions of the
Human Rights
Code
:

5(1) Every person has a right to equal treatment with
respect to employment without discrimination because of race,
ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin,
citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, age, record of
offences, marital status, family status or handicap.

. . . . .

10(1) In Part I and in this Part,

. . . . .

"because of handicap" means for the reason that the person
has or has had, or is believed to have or have had,

(a) any degree of physical disability . . . that is
caused by bodily injury, birth defect or illness
. . .

. . . . .

(e) an injury or disability for which benefits were
claimed or received under the Workers' Compensation
Act;

"equal" means subject to all requirements, qualifications and
considerations that are not a prohibited ground of
discrimination;

. . . . .

11(1) A right of a person under Part I is infringed where a
requirement, qualification or factor exists that is not
discrimination on a prohibited ground but that results in the
exclusion, restriction or preference of a group of persons
who are identified by a prohibited ground of discrimination
and of whom the person is a member, except where,

(a) the requirement, qualification or factor is reasonable
and bona fide in the circumstances; or

(b) it is declared in this Act, other than in section 17,
that to discriminate because of such ground is not an
infringement of a right.

(2) The Commission, the board of inquiry or a court shall
not find that a requirement, qualification or factor is
reasonable and bona fide in the circumstances unless it is
satisfied that the needs of the group of which the person is
a member cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the
person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering
the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and
safety requirements, if any.

. . . . .

17(1) A right of a person under this Act is not infringed
for the reason only that the person is incapable of
performing or fulfilling the essential duties or requirements
attending the exercise of the right because of handicap.

(2) The Commission, the board of inquiry or a court shall
not find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the
needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue
hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those
needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if
any, and health and safety requirements, if any.

ANALYSIS

Standard of Review

The collective agreement is subject to the dictates of the

Human Rights Code
. While parties to a collective agreement can
negotiate increased protection against discrimination, they
cannot contract out of those provisions of the Code that have
the effect of further protecting the human rights of the people
affected: N.A.P.E. v. Newfoundland,
1996 CanLII 190 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 3 at p. 15,
134 D.L.R. (4th) 1 at pp. 8-9. The parties agreed that since
the Board was interpreting and applying questions of general
law relating to the Code, the Board's decision is reviewable on
a standard of correctness: N.A.P.E., at p. 11 S.C.R., p. 5
D.L.R.

Employer Contributions to Benefit Premiums

(i) Direct discrimination under s. 5 of the Code

I have briefly set out the positions of the parties. It is
now necessary to set those arguments against the statutory
framework, beginning with the employer contributions to the
benefit plans. In Brooks v. Canada Safeway Ltd.,
1989 CanLII 96 (SCC)
, [1989] 1
S.C.R. 1219 at p. 1240, 59 D.L.R. (4th) 321 at p. 337, a case
concerned with discrimination on the basis of sex, Dickson
C.J.C., writing for the court, stated:

Increasingly, employee benefits plans have become part of the
terms and conditions of employment. Once an employer decides
to provide an employee benefit package, exclusions from such
schemes may not be made in a discriminatory fashion.
Selective compensation of this nature would clearly amount to
sex discrimination. Benefits available through employment
must be disbursed in a non-discriminatory manner.

(Emphasis added)

In this passage, the court identified employee benefit plans
as a form of compensation. In my view, employer contributions
to such plans are similarly a form of compensation. The
appellant provided no evidence to the contrary. Providing
different levels of compensation to different groups of
employees is not itself discriminatory within the meaning of
the Code. Prohibited discrimination only occurs when the
distinction is based on a prohibited ground. The prohibited
ground alleged in this case is "by reason of handicap" within
the meaning of s. 10. The appellant argues that the nurses are
denied this form of compensation because they are handicapped.
Thus, the violation of s. 5(1) of the Code is established. I do
not agree.

Disabled nurses do not receive this compensation because they
are not providing services to their employer. It is not
prohibited discrimination to distinguish for purposes of
compensation between employees who are providing services to
the employer and those who are not. It would be prohibited
discrimination for the employer to provide different
compensation to different groups of employees providing
services, if the distinction were based on a prohibited ground.
That was the problem in Brooks. Under the disability plan in
that case, employees who were unable to work due to sickness or
accident were provided with benefits or, in the words of
Dickson C.J.C., compensation. However, pregnant employees who
were unable to work in the 17-week period surrounding the birth
were excluded from the plan even when the reason for their
inability to work was unrelated to the pregnancy. Instead,
these employees were required to draw upon the less generous
pregnancy benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971,
S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48. The court found that this distinction,
drawn on the basis of pregnancy, was sex discrimination. A
critical element in finding discrimination was establishing the
appropriate comparator group. The employer argued that since
pregnancy is not a sickness or accident it need not treat
pregnant employees the same as employees who are unable to work
due to sickness or accident. Dickson C.J.C. rejected this
approach. Rather, he looked at the underlying rationale of the
disability plan, which he described at p. 1237 S.C.R., p. 334
D.L.R. as "the laudable desire to compensate persons who are
unable to work for valid health-related reasons". Having decided
to provide such a plan, the employer was not entitled to
distinguish between persons who are unable to work for valid
health-related reasons on the basis of sex.

The Supreme Court of Canada reached a similar conclusion in
Gibbs v. Battlefords District Co-operative Ltd.,
1996 CanLII 187 (SCC)
, [1996] 3
S.C.R. 566, 140 D.L.R. (4th) 1. In Gibbs, the plan provided
income replacement to employees rendered unable to work by
disability while they were incapable of returning to their
jobs. The plan, however, was discriminatory. It provided less
generous benefits for mental disability than for physical
disability. At issue was whether the appropriate comparison was
between the physically disabled and the mentally disabled -- in
which case the plan was discriminatory; or between the disabled
generally and the able-bodied -- in which case it was argued
there was no discrimination. Sopinka J., relying on Brooks,
wrote for the majority that the appropriate comparator group
could only be determined by looking at the purpose of the
disability plan (at p 588 S.C.R., pp. 16-17 D.L.R.):

The first step is to determine, in all the circumstances of
the case, the purpose of the disability plan. Comparing the
benefits allocated to employees pursuant to different
purposes is not helpful in determining discrimination -- it
is understandable that insurance benefits designed for
disparate purposes will differ. If, however, benefits are
allocated pursuant to the same purpose, yet benefits differ
as the result of characteristics that are not relevant to
this purpose, discrimination may well exist.

The purpose of the plan in Gibbs was to insure employees
against the income-related consequences of becoming disabled
and unable to work. Thus, it was appropriate to compare the
benefits received by one group of disabled with the disabled
generally, but not the workforce as a whole. Again, as in
Brooks, the employer was not obliged to provide this form of
income replacement, but having done so, it could not
discriminate between employees on a prohibited basis.

Similarly, in War Amputations of Canada v. Canada (1997),
1997 CanLII 872 (ON CA)
, 36
O.R. (3d) 709, 155 D.L.R. (4th) 125, this court held there was
no discrimination where veterans (primarily men) received
different pensions than their survivors (primarily women),
because the two different benefit schemes had different
purposes.

In the case presently before the court, the purpose of the
employer contributions to benefit plans is to provide an
additional form of compensation in exchange for work. Having
chosen to provide this form of compensation, the employer could
not discriminate on a prohibited basis. However, the employer
could distinguish based on the reason for providing the
compensation: work. On its face, discrimination would exist if
the employer provided different levels of compensation for work
because of handicap. Likewise, it would constitute
discrimination if the employer provided different levels of
compensation for not working because of handicap. But, in this
context it makes no sense to compare working employees with
those not working. As Sopinka J. said, comparing the benefits
allocated to employees pursuant to different purposes is not
helpful in determining discrimination.

I also do not find it helpful to attempt to isolate different
elements of the compensation package such as employer
contributions to premiums, vacation pay, and wages and ascribe
different purposes to each so as to create a discrimination
argument. They are all part of the compensation package
negotiated by the parties in exchange for work by the
employees. When the employee is not working, different
considerations and different forms of payment may apply. For
instance, employees may receive workers' compensation or long-
term disability payments.

In essence, the appellant's argument is that the income
replacement plans should include payment of these premiums.
This is a matter to be determined in the collective bargaining
process. It would only be covered by the
Human Rights Code
if
the income replacement plan itself discriminated on a
prohibited basis (as in Brooks and Gibbs). That is not the case
here. Leaving aside the difference between employees on
workers' compensation and those on long-term disability, which
is not properly before this court, the benefits provided to
handicap employees not providing work are more generous than to
other employees not providing work. Therefore, there is no
discrimination on a prohibited basis within the meaning of s.
5(1) of the Code. Accordingly, it is unnecessary to consider
whether the employers could rely upon the justification in s.
17 of the Code.

(ii) Constructive discrimination under s. 11 of the Code

The appellant also argues that the treatment of the disabled
employees in respect of benefits constitutes constructive or
adverse effect discrimination under s. 11. Section 11 was the
basis of Mr. Anand's dissent. He reasoned that the Board was
not bound by Versa Services as the Divisional Court had not
considered Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears
Ltd., supra, an adverse discrimination case. Simpsons-Sears was
decided under a predecessor to the Code that did not include s.
11. Nevertheless, McIntyre J., speaking for the court, held
that the Code prohibited adverse discrimination.

However, McIntyre J. also held that where adverse
discrimination is found, the working rule or condition found to
constitute adverse discrimination is not struck down, rather
some accommodation is required from the employer for the
benefit of the complainant. In the absence of a statutory duty
to accommodate, McIntyre J. fashioned a test that he considered
consistent with the intent of the Code; namely, the employer
must show that it has taken the reasonable steps toward
accommodation of the employee's position open to it without
undue hardship: Simpsons-Sears at pp. 556-60 S.C.R., pp. 336-38
D.L.R.

The legislature has now enacted provisions in the Code,
including s. 11, expressly dealing with constructive
discrimination. The decision in Versa Services refers to s. 11.
I cannot agree with Mr. Anand that the failure of the Versa
Services court to explicitly mention Simpsons-Sears provided
him with a basis for refusing to follow it. The principle of
adverse or constructive discrimination was clearly before the
court.

In any event, I am not satisfied that the appellant has
demonstrated a contravention of s. 11. In its factum, the
appellant put the case for a finding of constructive
discrimination under s. 11 in this way:

Where access to benefits in employment is at issue, adverse
effect discrimination is established when benefits otherwise
generally available to employees are limited or denied to
certain employees on the basis of a prohibited ground of
discrimination. Unequal treatment is identified by comparing
the situation of the group adversely affected because of a
protected ground with the group to whom the benefit is
generally available.

(Emphasis added)

In my view, this submission does not describe a violation of
s. 11 of the Code. Rather, the submission alleges direct
discrimination under s. 5, a submission that I have already
disposed of against the appellant. This does not, however, end
the matter. For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied that
even if the rule respecting employer contributions to benefit
plan premiums constitutes constructive discrimination, properly
understood, the justification in s. 11(1)(b) for a bona fide
occupational qualification (BFOQ) applies.

The starting point for properly understanding adverse effect
or constructive discrimination is Simpsons-Sears. In that case,
at p. 551 S.C.R., p. 332 D.L.R., McIntyre J. described adverse
effect or constructive discrimination in the following terms:

On the other hand, there is the concept of adverse effect
discrimination. It arises where an employer for genuine
business reasons adopts a rule or standard which is on its
face neutral, and which will apply equally to all employees,
but which has a discriminatory effect upon a prohibited
ground on one employee or group of employees in that it
imposes, because of some special characteristic of the
employee or group, obligations, penalties, or restrictive
conditions not imposed on other members of the work force
. . . An employment rule honestly made for sound economic or
business reasons, equally applicable to all to whom it is
intended to apply, may yet be discriminatory if it affects a
person or group of persons differently from others to whom it
may apply.

Adverse effect discrimination as explained in Simpsons-Sears
and constructive discrimination as codified in s. 11 appear to
cover the same ground. Both concepts are premised on a neutral
rule or standard that applies equally to all employees but has
a discriminatory effect because it imposes a penalty on a group
because of some group characteristic protected by the Code.

In Simpsons-Sears, the neutral rule was the requirement that
all employees work on Friday evenings on a rotating basis and
on two Saturdays out of three. The discriminatory effect in
Simpsons-Sears occurred because of the employee's religious
practices. The complainant became a member of the Seventh-Day
Adventist Church. A tenet of that faith is that the Sabbath,
which extends from sundown Friday to sundown Saturday, must be
strictly kept. The neutral rule would have a differing impact
on different groups of employees. For example, employees with
children would be unable to spend time with their children
Friday evening and Saturday. The impact upon the complainant
was that she would be unable to comply with the tenets of her
religion if required to work at those times. The discriminatory
effect occurs in the latter and not the former because the
adverse impact in Simpsons-Sears resulted from the exercise of
religion. Discrimination on the basis of religion (creed under
the Code) is prohibited. In s. 11 terms, the Simpsons-Sears
complainant was a member of a group identified by a prohibited
ground of discrimination.

In this case, the neutral rule (a requirement, qualification
or factor in the words of s. 11) may be stated as follows: the
employer contributes toward premium coverage of participating
eligible nurses in the "active employ" of the hospital. While
stating the neutral rule is relatively simple, describing the
discriminatory effect, especially in disability cases, is more
problematic. In Versa Services, the arbitrator found no s. 11
constructive discrimination by adopting a narrow, policy-driven
interpretation of constructive discrimination in cases of
handicap. He reached this conclusion by reading ss. 11 and 17
together. For convenience, these sections are set out below:

11(1) A right of a person under Part I is infringed where a
requirement, qualification or factor exists that is not
discrimination on a prohibited ground but that results in the
exclusion, restriction or preference of a group of persons
who are identified by a prohibited ground of discrimination
and of whom the person is a member, except where,

(a) the requirement, qualification or factor is reasonable
and bona fide in the circumstances; or

(b) it is declared in this Act, other than in section 17,
that to discriminate because of such ground is not an
infringement of a right.

(2) The Commission, the board of inquiry or a court shall
not find that a requirement, qualification or factor is
reasonable and bona fide in the circumstances unless it is
satisfied that the needs of the group of which the person is
a member cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the
person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering
the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and
safety requirements, if any.

. . . . .

17(1) A right of a person under this Act is not infringed
for the reason only that the person is incapable of
performing or fulfilling the essential duties or requirements
attending the exercise of the right because of handicap.

(2) The Commission, the board of inquiry or a court shall
not find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the
needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue
hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those
needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if
any, and health and safety requirements, if any.

By reading s. 11 with s. 17, the Versa Services arbitrator
found that in cases of handicap, s. 11 treats matters of
compensation differently from participation. His reasoning is
summarized in the following passages at pp. 203-04:

In my view, the Code treats compensation differently from
participation. The reference in s. 17 to a person's
capability to perform duties indicates this section applies
to engagement in active employment. On this front, s. 17
adopts the broader notion of equal treatment which requires
differences to be accommodated, so as not to exclude a
handicapped person from a work place. Section 17 cannot be
construed as applying the same broad notion of equal
treatment to compensation because it contains no reference to
compensation. . . .

In coming to this conclusion, I have not overlooked s. 11
of the Code which adopts a broad understanding of equal
treatment . . . Section 17 is addressed exclusively to
handicap. This section requires special treatment to enable
people with disabilities to participate in active employment,
but stops short of requiring special compensation measures.
This deliberate omission in a section dealing specifically
with handicap should not be negated by a broad reading of the
more general requirements of s. 11 which addresses all of the
prohibited grounds of discrimination.

(Emphasis added)

I cannot agree with this interpretation of s. 11. Such an
interpretation would offer less protection to one historically
disadvantaged group (the disabled) than another and a group for
whom adverse effects discrimination is "especially relevant":
Eldridge v. British Columbia (Attorney General),
1997 CanLII 327 (SCC)
, [1997] 3
S.C.R. 624 at p. 672, 151 D.L.R. (4th) 577. That interpretation
is also inconsistent with the history and plain wording of the
provisions.

The predecessors to ss. 11 and 17 were
ss. 10
and
16
of the

Human Rights Code
, S.O. 1981, c. 53. Section 10 dealt with
constructive discrimination and like s. 11 of the present Code,
provided a justification in cl. (a) for a bona fide requirement
or qualification or in cl. (b) where "it is declared in this
Act that to discriminate because of such ground is not an
infringement of a right". Unlike s. 11, there was no express
duty to accommodate in s. 10. Section 16 dealt with handicap in
two respects. Section 16(1)(a) deemed inability to access
premises, services, goods, facilities or accommodation by
reason of handicap not to be an infringement of the Code.
Section 16(1)(b) was identical to present s. 17(1). Again,
unlike the present s. 17, there was no express duty to
accommodate the handicapped individual.

The present versions of ss. 11 and 17 were enacted by the
Equality Rights Statute Law Amendment Act, 1986, S.O. 1986, c.
64. Notably, the long title of that Act is: "An Act to amend
certain Ontario Statutes to conform to
section 15
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
".

A duty to accommodate was added to s. 11 as now set out in s.
11(2) and the words "other than in section 17" were added to
the present s. 11(1)(b). Section 17 was substantially amended.
The defence in former s. 16(1)(a) was repealed and a duty to
accommodate was added to what is now s. 17(2). It seems to me
that the repeal of s. 16(1)(a) demonstrated the legislature's
concern that, in light of
s. 15
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
, one historically disadvantaged group (the
disabled) could not continue to be treated differently than
other historically disadvantaged groups. The fact that the
legislature nevertheless maintained a special justification for
some differences based on handicap recognizes the reality that
unfair discrimination of the disabled is not always grounded in
negative stereotypes. In many circumstances equality of
treatment of the disabled depends upon an assessment of the
capabilities of the individual, not the group. Sopinka J. descr
ibed these two different objectives of human rights legislation
for the disabled in Eaton v. Brant County Board of Education,

1997 CanLII 366 (SCC)
, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 241 at pp. 272-73, 142 D.L.R. (4th) 385,
where, in relation to
s. 15(1)
of the Charter, he said the
following:

The principal object of certain of the prohibited grounds
is the elimination of discrimination by the attribution of
untrue characteristics based on stereotypical attitudes
relating to immutable conditions such as race or sex. In the
case of disability, this is one of the objectives. The other
equally important objective seeks to take into account the
true characteristics of this group which act as headwinds to
the enjoyment of society's benefits and to accommodate them.
Exclusion from the mainstream of society results from the
construction of a society based solely on "mainstream"
attributes to which disabled persons will never be able to
gain access. Whether it is the impossibility of success at a
written test for a blind person, or the need for ramp access
to a library, the discrimination does not lie in the
attribution of untrue characteristics to the disabled
individual. The blind person cannot see and the person in a
wheelchair needs a ramp. Rather, it is the failure to make
reasonable accommodation, to fine-tune society so that its
structures and assumptions do not result in the relegation and
banishment of disabled persons from participation, which
results in discrimination against them. The discrimination
inquiry which uses "the attribution of stereotypical
characteristics" reasoning as commonly understood is simply
inappropriate here. It may be seen rather as a case of reverse
stereotyping which, by not allowing for the condition of a
disabled individual, ignores his or her disability and forces
the individual to sink or swim within the mainstream
environment. It is recognition of the actual characteristics,
and reasonable accommodation of these characteristics which is
the central purpose of s. 15(1) in relation to disability.

(Emphasis added)

However, the fact that the legislature provided for this
individual assessment in s. 17 cannot mean that the handicapped
can be deprived of the protections available under s. 11 where
there has been constructive discrimination of the disabled as a
group. The legislature has expressly exempted s. 17 as a
justification for constructive discrimination against a group
under s. 11. It would be a strange result if courts or
tribunals were able to avoid this legislative choice by simply
adopting a narrow reading of s. 11.

I also cannot accept the distinction drawn in Versa Services
between participation and compensation. The Supreme Court has
recognized that constructive discrimination in matters of
compensation is prohibited in relation to religion under the
comparable legislation in Quebec in Chambly, Commission
scolaire régionale v. Bergevin,
1994 CanLII 102 (SCC)
, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 525, 115 D.L.R.
(4th) 609. In that case, constructive discrimination was
established because Jewish teachers, although allowed to be
absent for religious holy days, were not paid. The calendar or
work schedule had a discriminatory effect since the religious
holy days of the majority were recognized as holidays from work
and thus they did not lose any pay. The school board was
therefore under a duty to accommodate the Jewish teachers short
of undue hardship. The Supreme Court easily found that the
board had not met this duty because the collective agreement
expressly provided that teachers could be absent yet paid for
other "valid" reasons.

If, as would appear to be the case, s. 11 covers constructive
discrimination in matters of compensation for one group with
protected rights under the Code, I fail to see the basis for
exempting another group, the disabled, from its protection in
those matters. This does not mean that there is no
justification for such distinctions, only that the
justification for apparently discriminatory treatment of the
group must take place within s. 11 and specifically within the
duty to accommodate as set out in s. 11(1)(a) and (2). The s.
11 analysis must also take into account the different
objectives of the prohibited grounds of discrimination as
explained by Sopinka J. in Eaton. In particular, although s. 11
makes no express reference to capacity, capacity is a central
concept in analyzing the duty to accommodate the handicapped,
whether it is under s. 11 or s. 17. Section 17 gives an
employer a justification for direct discrimination on the basis
of handicap under s. 5 where the indiv idual is incapable and
that individual cannot be accommodated short of undue hardship.
It would make no sense that an employer faces a heavier burden
in cases of constructive discrimination under s. 11. Anne
Molloy made a similar point in "Disability and the Duty to
Accommodate" (1992), 1 Cdn. Lab. L.J. 23 at p. 36 in her
discussion of Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human
Rights Commission),
1990 CanLII 76 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 489, 72 D.L.R. (4th) 417:

If logic is to prevail, it must be the case that the analysis
of direct discrimination in the presence of a BFOQ [bona fide
occupational qualification] as set out by Wilson J. will in
the end result require the same kind of accommodation as
would be the case for indirect discrimination. Otherwise, the
result of Wilson J.'s analysis would be that an employer has
a heavier onus to discharge in cases of adverse impact
discrimination than in cases of direct discrimination. This
is, at best, an anomalous result. If the test actually
develops in this way, we will be faced with the ridiculous
situation of victims of discrimination arguing that the
employer was acting unintentionally in applying a general
neutral rule which had an unfortunate disparate effect on
persons with disabilities (so that the duty of accommodation
will clearly apply). On the other hand, employers will seek
to establish that the rule in question was direct
discrimination against disabled people (so that the duty to
accommodate is less clear). This, too, would be an untenable
result.

The need to avoid this anomalous result is all the more
important for the disabled since as Molloy points out, at p.
37, with respect to disability-based discrimination "the line
between the two kinds of discrimination is much more blurred"
than it is with respect, for example, to religious-based
discrimination. The result can be avoided by focusing on the
objectives of the prohibition on disability-based
discrimination as explained by Sopinka J. Molloy makes the same
point at p. 26:

The accommodation of differences for persons with
disabilities therefore requires overcoming the ignorance,
stereotypical attitudes and paternalism that are the source
of much of the overt disability discrimination. But
overcoming the attitudinal problems of employers and society
in general is only one part of the accommodation required by
persons with disabilities. The other key component is the
physical accommodation of the special needs of the disabled
worker.

To summarize, s. 11 applies to constructive discrimination on
the basis of handicap and includes discrimination in
compensation. The duty to accommodate the group under s. 11(2)
may, however, involve elements similar to the elements of the
analysis of the duty to accommodate the individual in cases of
direct discrimination under s. 17.

In my view, it is possible to find that the neutral rule in
this case has a discriminatory effect within the meaning of s.
11(1). To repeat, the neutral rule may be stated as follows:
the employer contributes toward premium coverage of
participating eligible nurses in the active employ of the
hospital. This rule has the effect of requiring the group of
employees identified by the prohibited ground of discrimination
to assume the burden of paying the entire contributions for
benefits if they wish to maintain coverage. Admittedly, these
employees are treated no differently than other employees on
unpaid leave of absence, the difference is that these employees
are adversely affected by the rule because of their disability.
The issue then is whether the employers are entitled to the
BFOQ justification in s. 11(1)(b). In my view, they are. I
reach this conclusion not because of the distinction drawn in
Versa Services between compensation and participation, but
rather by having regard to the n ature of the accommodation
required for this kind of constructive discrimination.

An example may assist in understanding the problem. Assume
that an employer changes from paying its employees wages based
on hours worked to paying on the basis of the number of pieces
produced. Assume further that the disabled employees are simply
unable to produce as many pieces as the able-bodied employees
and as a result their wages are reduced. Arguably, this
constitutes constructive discrimination. The facially neutral
standard of paying by the number of pieces produced results in
a restriction on the ability of the disabled employees to earn
the same wages as the able-bodied employees. In accordance with
s. 11(1)(a), the employer could justify the different result by
showing that this standard was reasonable and bona fide in the
circumstances. However, in accordance with s. 11(2), the board
of inquiry or court is only entitled to find that the standard
is reasonable and bona fide if it is satisfied that the needs
of the group cannot be accommodated without undue hardship
considering the "cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and
health and safety requirements, if any". Nevertheless, I do not
read s. 11(2) as imposing upon the employer the burden of
simply topping up the wages of the disabled employees. That, in
my view, is not the type of accommodation contemplated by s.
11(2) and in fact is inimical to the principles underlying the
Code. To quote again from Sopinka J. in Eaton at pp. 272-73:

The discrimination inquiry which uses "the attribution of
stereotypical characteristics" reasoning as commonly
understood is simply inappropriate here. It may be seen
rather as a case of reverse stereotyping which, by not
allowing for the condition of a disabled individual, ignores
his or her disability and forces the individual to sink or
swim within the mainstream environment. It is recognition of
the actual characteristics, and reasonable accommodation of
these characteristics which is the central purpose of s.
15(1) in relation to disability.

(Emphasis added)

Simply topping up the wages of the disabled employees and
paying them as if they are not disabled is nothing more than
reverse stereotyping as described by Sopinka J. Rather, it
would seem to me that the employer in this hypothetical must
attempt to accommodate the group. For example, the employer may
provide devices and instruments that would allow the disabled
employees to perform close to the same level as the able-bodied
employees. The duty is on the employer to take all steps short
of undue hardship to accommodate the needs of the person
discriminated against so that they can compete equally with the
other employees. It is by attempting to accommodate their
actual characteristics so as to bring them within the workplace
environment that the employer complies with the Code. This
point is made in the Report of the Commission on Equality in
Employment (October 1984) (the Abella Report) at pp. 39-40 and
42:

The issue must be examined from the point of view of the
individual who has the disability rather than from the point
of view of the assumptions of the employer. This is not to
suggest that an employer's needs and concerns are not
relevant; in fact, they may be critically so. But it is to
suggest that the way one deals with this issue is first to
determine what measures are necessary to maximize the ability
of a qualified disabled individual to perform the job for
which he or she is being employed. The determination must be
made individual by individual. Disabled persons do not expect
to be hired for a job they cannot or could not be trained to
do. What they are entitled to expect, however, is that
wherever reasonably possible employers make adjustments to
workplaces so that disabled persons are not handicapped in
their ability to perform the job.

. . . . .

Although there was general agreement that wherever possible
incentives should be provided to employers to accommodate
people with disabilities, including tax deductions to
retrofit premises, hire support personnel, and make available
technical aids, there was also general agreement that wage
subsidies were degrading.

(Emphasis added)

It may be that this goal cannot be fully accomplished and
that short of undue hardship the employer, for example, can
provide technical aids that will only partly bring the disabled
employee to the same level as able-bodied employees. However,
in my view, that is all the Code requires the employer to do.
The employer is not required to abandon the standard (assuming
it to be a BFOQ) and pay the disabled employees according to
some different standard. Obviously, it may do so voluntarily,
but this is not what the Code requires.

The appellant, in this case, does not seek any reasonable
accommodation or modification of the rule for the actual
characteristics of its disabled members. Indeed, in this case,
there is no modification or accommodation possible. The
appellant asks, in effect, that the rule as set out in the
collective agreement be struck down. In Simpsons-Sears,
McIntyre J. pointed out the important distinction in remedies
depending on whether the allegation is direct or adverse effect
discrimination. The Supreme Court of Canada has applied that
reasoning in subsequent cases. For example in Central Alberta
Dairy Pool, at pp. 506-07 S.C.R., p. 428 D.L.R., Wilson J. held
as follows:

Where the rule established by the employer fits into the
category of "direct discrimination" and is not saved by any
statutory justification, it is simply struck down. The
example cited by McIntyre J. was Etobicoke. In that case the
mandatory retirement rule discriminated directly on the basis
of age and the employer's evidence was inadequate to
establish a BFOQ. The rule was struck down. Where a neutral
rule has an adverse discriminatory effect, the same result
does not obtain. At p. 333 of [Simpsons-Sears] McIntyre J.
contrasts the approach taken to direct discrimination with
that taken to adverse effect discrimination:

No question arises in a case involving direct
discrimination. Where a working rule or condition of
employment is found to be discriminatory on a prohibited
ground and fails to meet any statutory justification test,
it is simply struck down: see the Etobicoke case, supra. In
the case of discrimination on the basis of creed resulting
from the effect of a condition or rule rationally related
to the performance of the job and not on its face
discriminatory, a different result follows. The working
rule or condition is not struck down, but its effect on the
complainant must be considered, and if the purpose of the

Ontario Human Rights Code
is to be given effect some
accommodation must be required from the employer for the
benefit of the complainant.

(Emphasis added)

Assuming that the rule respecting employer contributions to
benefits plans constitutes constructive discrimination, I am
satisfied that the justification in s. 11(1)(b) applies.
Requiring work in exchange for compensation is a reasonable and
bona fide requirement. There is no suggestion that the employer
can do anything to accommodate the needs of this group or
modify the requirement to place them in a position where they
can perform the work. Further, as I have not found direction
discrimination under s. 5, the rule in the collective agreement
stands.

Service Accrual

The discussion concerning employer contributions applies
equally to service accrual. The purpose of service accrual is
to fix the level of compensation on the salary grid and
vacation pay. Accordingly, for the purposes of s. 5, the
appropriate comparator group is other employees on unpaid leave
of absence. All employees within this group, handicapped and
non-handicapped, are treated the same. Hence, there is no s. 5
discrimination.

As regards constructive or adverse discrimination, for the
reasons set out above in relation to contributions to benefits
plans, there is no violation of s. 11. Again, as I understand
the agreed facts, these employees are on long-term disability
because they are unable to provide any service. Thus, there is
no amount of accommodation that the employer could provide that
would overcome the fundamental problem that these employees are
unable to work. This term of the collective agreement is not in
breach of the Code.

Accumulation of Seniority

Under this collective agreement, accrual of seniority has a
different purpose than service accrual or employer
contributions to benefit premiums. At pp. 55 and 56 of his
decision, Mr. Mitchnik points out that the situation may well
be different in other collective agreements. This agreement
sets out the purpose of seniority accrual:

10.06(c)  Nurses shall be selected for positions under either
10.06(a) or (b) [permanent vacancies and transfers]
on the basis of their skill, ability, experience and
qualifications. Where these factors are relatively
equal amongst the nurses considered, seniority shall
govern providing the successful applicant, if any, is
qualified to perform the available work within an
appropriate familiarization period.

. . . . .

10.07(a)  A layoff of nurses shall be made on the basis of
seniority provided that the nurses who are entitled
to remain on the basis of seniority are qualified to
perform the available work. Subject to the foregoing
nurses shall be first laid off.

Nurses shall be recalled in the order of seniority,
unless otherwise agreed between the Hospital and
local Association, provided that the nurse is
qualified to perform the available work.

To summarize, in this agreement, seniority is a consideration
for the purpose of filling vacancies and determining the order
in which employees are laid off and hired back. However,
seniority is not the only consideration. The seniority clause
in this agreement is a competitive clause: see Arthurs, Carter,
Fudge, Glasbeek and Trudeau, Labour Law and Industrial
Relations in Canada, 4th ed. (1993) at p. 342. The principal
considerations for filling vacancies are skill, ability,
experience and qualifications. Seniority is only the deciding
factor where these other considerations are relatively equal
among the competing employees. Similarly, for layoffs and
recalls, seniority only governs if the most senior employees
are qualified to perform the available work.

Thus, in this agreement, seniority is not directly related to
compensation. The purpose of seniority is not to provide an
additional form of compensation in exchange for work. Unlike
service accrual, for example, years of seniority do not
determine the employee's compensation. Rather, the seniority
provisions are triggered simply by the status of being an
employee, a status long-term disabled employees retain. It
follows that the relevant comparator group with respect to
seniority is all other employees.

It has been said that seniority is "labour's premier equity
tool and should be respected as such": the Abella Report at p.
220. "Seniority is a neutral system that is colour-blind,
gender-blind, and age-blind . . . It also offers those with
physical limitations the opportunity to insist on the right to
try to perform a job.": P. Nash, L. Gottheil, "Employment
Equity: A Union Perspective" (1992), 2 Can. Lab. L.J. 49 at p.
54. The seniority provisions in this agreement appear to be
directed to achieving fairness in competition for promotions,
lay-offs and call-backs. Nevertheless, even bona fide seniority
systems can have discriminatory potential.

So far as possible, seniority systems should be developed
through the collective bargaining process. However, where
collective bargaining produces an agreement that contravenes
the statutory protections, the arbitrator or the court, as the
case may be, has an obligation to intervene and the employer
has a duty to accommodate within the statutory limits. The
affected griever need not show that there was an intention to
discriminate: Simpsons-Sears, at p. 548 S.C.R., pp. 329-30
D.L.R.; Eldridge v. British Columbia (Attorney General), at p.
671.

In this agreement, seniority directly affects the ability of
employees to access, remain in, and thrive in the workplace. It
is therefore a right that is at the core of human rights
legislation as it affects the disabled. M. David Lepofsky notes
that while the public considers current unemployment rates
running between 7 and 9 per cent to be intolerably high,
working-aged disabled persons have confronted extremely high
unemployment rates, rates that are several times those for the
able-bodied: "The Duty to Accommodate: A Purposive Approach"
(1992), 1 Cdn. Lab. L.J. 1 at p. 10. [See Note 1 at end of
document.] Despite advances aimed at increasing the employability
of disabled persons, they still encounter "massive barriers" when
seeking jobs. Persons with disabilities have "too often been
excluded from the labour force . . . [and] subjected to invidious
stereotyping". In comparison to non-disabled they are "more
likely to be outside the labour force, face much higher
unemployment rates, and are concentrated at the lower end of t he
pay scale when employed": Eldridge v. British Columbia (Attorney
General), at p. 668. Mr. Lepofsky argues, at p. 20, that the
different treatment required by the legislated duty to
accommodate is but a "modest means for attaining for the
accommodated worker equality of treatment in the workplace --
that is, the same opportunity to obtain and retain a job at that
place of employment that other workers enjoy. Indeed, this
prerequisite is a sine qua non of the duty to accommodate."

Disabled workers meeting the Code definition of handicapped,
who become disabled in the course of their employment and
perhaps as a result of the employment, will be more likely to
require an unpaid leave of absence. Depriving those employees
of their seniority during those periods of absence in excess of
one year makes them increasingly vulnerable to layoff and also
less able to compete equally for promotions.

The right to accrue seniority is also at the core of the
disabled employee's ability to integrate into the workforce. As
the Abella Report points out at pp. 45-46:

It is not just the opportunity of becoming employed that is
at issue, it is the opportunity, once employed, of being able
to move through a corporation with the same facility as would
any other employee with a disabled individual's
qualifications. The danger for members of any of the
designated groups is that, once hired, there will be an
assumption by employers that the responsibility has been
discharged and that promotion, training, or other corporate
opportunities will be denied for the same reasons that
original employment itself might have been denied. The
stereotypes must be confronted not only at the point of entry
to the corporation, but throughout its systems and practices
and at every level. There should be a presumption in favour
of a "duty of reasonable accommodation" so that employment
barriers are eliminated and access to the fullest range of
employment opportunities is available.

(Emphasis added)

Under this collective agreement, where candidates for a job
vacancy are relatively equal in all other respects, seniority
breaks the tie. As Mr. Lepofsky states at p. 7:

. . . the duty to accommodate serves to enable individuals to
have their qualifications and competence to contribute to the
workplace evaluated in a fair and accurate manner. When an
employer seeks to determine whether a particular candidate
for a job is qualified to do that job, the aim of the
exercise is to ascertain as effectively as possible the
individual's true capabilities -- to identify what kinds of
positive contributions this person could make to the
workplace. It is vital that such an appraisal be carried out
in a fair and accurate manner, both from the perspective of
effective business decision-making and from the vantage-point
of the job applicant.

By depriving employees of seniority accrual for the periods
when they were unable to work, disabled employees are put at an
unfair disadvantage, by reason of their handicap. Under this
agreement, seniority accumulates from the date of last hire.
After the nurse has successfully completed the probationary
period, which is calculated on the basis of tours or hours
actually worked (para. 10.01(a)), seniority for full-time
employees involves nothing more than the passage of time as an
employee. [See Note 2 at end of document.] However, while
employees on active service accumulate seniority from the date of
last hire, handicapped employees cease accumulating seniority one
year after they become disabled.

Seniority is of consequence under this agreement when the
disabled employees have returned, or seek to return, to active
service and are in competition with other employees on active
service. Thus, having regard to the purpose of seniority in
this agreement, the appropriate comparator group is the
employees as a whole. Disabled employees are denied rights
given to other employees in a manner constituting
discrimination within the meaning of s. 5 of the Code.

Having found direct discrimination within the meaning of s.
5, it is necessary to consider the effect of s. 17 of the Code.
To repeat, s. 17 provides as follows:

17(1) A right of a person under this Act is not infringed
for the reason only that the person is incapable of
performing or fulfilling the essential duties or requirements
attending the exercise of the right because of handicap.

(2) The Commission, the board of inquiry or a court shall
not find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the
needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue
hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those
needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if
any, and health and safety requirements, if any.

In my view, s. 17 does not excuse this violation of s. 5. We
were not referred to any training, additional qualification, or
particular on-the-job experience that is necessary to enable a
nurse to continue to accumulate seniority. Put another way, it
has not been shown that while on long-term disability, the
employee is incapable of performing any essential duty or
requirement relating to the accumulation of seniority in this
agreement. In Charter s. 15 terms, the collective agreement
relies upon a distinction that is irrelevant to the functional
values underlying the seniority system: Eldridge v. British
Columbia (Attorney General), at p. 670. Seniority for full-time
employees involves nothing more than the passage of time as an
employee -- a status that long-term disabled persons retain.
Moreover, once the employees return to work, if they are less
qualified to perform the work for any sought-after promotion,
the fact that they have greater seniority than other competing
employees does not matter. Similarly, their greater seniority
will not protect them from lay-offs or guarantee their return
to work if they are not capable of performing the available
work. Simply put, I can see no essential duties or requirements
attending the exercise of the right that the employee cannot
fulfill while on unpaid leave of absence by reason of handicap.

The position of the disabled employees under s. 17 with
respect to seniority can usefully be compared with their
position with respect to service accrual or contributions to
benefits, if I had found direct discrimination in relation to
those compensation-related rights. While they are disabled,
these handicapped employees cannot provide their labour, an
essential requirement for receiving compensation.
Discriminatory provisions in this collective agreement
affecting compensation, such as accrual of service, or
providing forms of compensation, such as employer contributions
to benefits, would therefore be excused by s. 17. In contrast,
the seniority provisions cannot be justified by s. 17, since
those provisions do not depend upon the employee providing
labour, but are triggered simply by the status of being an
employee.

I am also impressed by the reasons of the experienced Chair
of this arbitration panel, Mr. Mitchnick. He points out the
different purposes of seniority as opposed to matters related
to compensation, in part, as follows:

That deals with both the benefits and the "service" issues.
"Seniority", on the other hand, more typically is a term
used under a collective agreement to define the relationship
of employees inter se . . . . While it might be argued that
there is no more reason to allow the accumulation of
"seniority" credits than "service" credits when an
employee is not actually working, there does tend to be a
recognizable distinction in the two situations with respect
to the relative extent of the employer's interest (as the
current collective agreement itself reflects) . . . .

. . . . .

The question thus is this: given the relatively limited
interest of the employer (as distinct from the "compensation"
issues), does it seem more probable than not that the
Legislature intended to create a protection against someone
forced off work for months or even years with, for example,
an injury suffered at their workplace, or engaged in a battle
with cancer, upon their return having their "date of hire"
effectively adjusted forward, so that they are more likely,
as in this case, to be exposed to lay-off than individuals
who came to the employer at some point after them? We think
it entirely probable that it did. And, as can be seen in
those terms, the issue of seniority is, as the Association
urges, one much more closely aligned to the issue of
"access", than to the issue of "compensation" that we have
found to be governed by the Versa Services line of cases.

(Emphasis in original)

I also find support for this conclusion in the automatic
termination cases. There is a close analogy between denial of
seniority rights and automatic termination. In both cases, the
clause, even if viewed as facially neutral, has the capacity to
deprive the disabled worker of employment due to innocent
absence because of handicap: Ontario Nurses' Assn. v. Etobicoke
General Hospital, supra, at pp. 42-43.

For these reasons, I cannot agree with the Divisional Court
that the reasoning in Versa Services governs seniority rights.

As the provisions denying handicapped workers the right to
accumulate seniority while on long-term disability violate s. 5
and cannot be excused under s. 17, in accordance with Simpsons-
Sears, those provisions must be struck down.

If I am wrong, and the seniority provisions of this agreement
do not constitute direct discrimination under s. 5, I would
find that the provisions constitute constructive discrimination
under s. 11. The provisions impose the burden of loss of
seniority after one year's absence upon a group identified by a
prohibited ground of discrimination, namely, disability. This
is a burden not imposed on most other employees. For many of
the same reasons that I have found s. 17 does not excuse direct
discrimination, I would hold that these provisions do not
constitute a bona fide requirement or qualification within the
meaning of s. 11(l)(a). Pursuant to s. 11(2), a court cannot
find that a requirement or qualification is reasonable and bona
fide in the circumstances "unless it is satisfied that the
needs of the group of which the person is a member cannot be
accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible
for accommodating those needs".

In my view, when dealing with seniority in the context of a
collective agreement such as this, both the employer and the
union are responsible for accommodating these needs: Central
Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud,
1992 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970
at p. 989, 95 D.L.R. (4th) 577. The union in this case
obviously makes no claim that the members of the group cannot
be accommodated short of undue hardship.

The employer adduced no evidence with respect to the statutory
undue hardship factors of cost, [See Note 3 at end of document.]
outside sources of funding, and health and safety requirements.
The principal impact of changing the seniority rules in this type
of collective agreement is on the other employees. Restoring
seniority for the disabled employees affects the economic
security and promotion opportunities of those able-bodied nurses
who had benefited from the loss of seniority of the disabled
employees in accordance with the collective agreement. In Central
Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, the court considered
an argument that the accommodation necessary to take into account
the complainant's religious observances would adversely impact on
other employees. Sopinka J. held that more than minor
inconvenience must be shown before the right to accommodation
could be defeated. Speaking particularly of the impact on other
employees he wrote at pp. 984-85:

The employer must establish that actual interference with the
rights of other employees, which is not trivial but
substantial, will result from the adoption of the
accommodating measures. Minor interference or inconvenience
is the price to be paid for religious freedoms in a
multicultural society.

Assuming impact on other employees is a proper factor under
s. 11, I would apply the same reasoning to the accommodation of
the seniority rules for the disabled. Adjusting the seniority
rules to remove discriminatory effects can advance the element
of equity implied in using the neutral factor of length of
employment for calculating seniority. In my view, the
appropriate accommodation is to exempt employees covered by
this collective agreement from the provisions curtailing the
accumulation of seniority, throughout the period that the nurse
remains an employee and falls within the Code definition of
handicap: Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, at
p. 986.

THE RECORD

Finally, I should not leave this appeal without expressing a
concern with the record in this case. I have reached these
conclusions based on the very brief agreed facts and the
collective agreement itself. As I stated at the beginning of
these reasons, the parties led no evidence about the purpose of
the various impugned provisions. Similarly, no evidence was led
as to the potential consequences on other employees. For
instance, in oral argument counsel for the respondents
submitted that many employees on long-term disability are kept
on the employment roles essentially for purposes completely
unrelated to their status as employees. This preserves for the
employee the appearance of employment, the possibility (no
matter how remote) to return to work, and the social benefit of
a tie to the workforce and the friends in the bargaining unit.
These benefits are at virtually no cost to the employer.
However, if the appellants were successful in this appeal, at
some point it may be to the economic advantage of t he employer
to terminate these handicapped employees and exclude them from
the benefits of employee status. Even the modest accommodation
for seniority mandated by the award in this case may lead
employers to attempt to terminate the employment relationship
where the length of the absence "undermines" the employment
relationship or makes the relationship "no longer viable":
Brown and Beatty, Canadian Labour Arbitration, 3rd ed. (Aurora:
Canada Law Book, 1998) paragraphs 7:3210 and 7:3220. This is
just one of many troubling examples raised in oral argument on
which no evidence was led.

In my view, a more complete record would have been of
considerable assistance in resolving the issues on this appeal.
Such a record would, moreover, have been more consistent with
determining issues under a statute like the
Human Rights Code
,
that has almost quasi-constitutional status. Although the
following comments from MacKay v. Manitoba,
1989 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R.
357, 61 D.L.R. (4th) 385 at p. 388 were made in reasons for
judgment under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
they have application to a case such as this:

Charter
cases will frequently be concerned with concepts
and principles that are of fundamental importance to Canadian
society. For example, issues pertaining to freedom of
religion, freedom of expression and the right to life,
liberty and the security of the individual will have to be
considered by the courts. Decisions on these issues must be
carefully considered, as they will profoundly affect the
lives of Canadians and all residents of Canada. In light of
the importance and the impact that these decisions may have
in the future, the courts have every right to expect and
indeed to insist upon the careful preparation and
presentation of a factual basis in most Charter cases. The
relevant facts put forward may cover a wide spectrum dealing
with scientific, social, economic and political aspects.
Often expert opinion as to the future impact of the impugned
legislation and the result of the possible decisions
pertaining to it may be of great assistance to the courts.

Charter decisions should not and must not be made in a
factual vacuum. To attempt to do so would trivialize the

Charter
and inevitably result in ill-considered opinions. The
presentation of facts is not, as stated by the respondent, a
mere technicality; rather, it is essential to a proper
consideration of Charter issues.

(Emphasis added)

However, the parties urged us to decide this case on the
basis of the record, such as it is, and I have, with some
reluctance, done so.

DISPOSITION

Accordingly, I would allow the appeal in part and restore the
award of the Board of Arbitration. As success was divided, I
would not make any order for costs either of this appeal,
including the motion for leave to appeal, or of the appeal to
the Divisional Court.

Appeal allowed in part.
